title: The evening adhkar
tomorrow: she planned to read the whole Qur'an over break. it's day four. now?

segments.voice: Last week built the frame, all five posts, and ended with 'Isha: night, then rest. This week fills in what goes between them, starting at dusk.

Dusk on a porch in Houston: the streetlights blink on one by one, a dog two houses down won't stop barking, and Dadi's lips are moving. The morning has its words, and so does the evening. Amira sits down beside her and waits. When Dadi finishes, she tells a story instead of explaining. A man comes to the Prophet ﷺ one morning, in pain. Last night, he says, a scorpion stung me. And the Prophet's answer isn't about the scorpion at all.
screen: `STREETLIGHTS BLINK ON.` → `DADI'S LIPS ARE MOVING.` → `LAST NIGHT, A SCORPION.`

segments.voice: It's about the evening before. In the report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: had you said, when evening came, I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He created, it would not have harmed you. That's one of the evening adhkar, the remembrances for the end of the day. They mirror the morning ones. In the morning: we have entered the morning, and the dominion belongs to God. At dusk, in another report in Sahih Muslim: we have entered the evening, and the dominion belongs to God. Same sentence, turned toward the dark. And in Abu Dawud, the Prophet tells a companion to recite the short chapter that begins, in Pickthall's words, "Say: He is Allah, the One!" along with the two chapters of refuge after it, three times at evening and at morning, and they will be enough for him. Notice what kind of words these are. They aren't asking for a good grade or a lucky night. They're asking for shelter, the thing a person wants most when the light goes: a door that locks, a name to say in the dark. Dadi doesn't say them because the porch is dangerous. She says them because the day is ending, and she'd rather end it held.
screen: `HAD YOU SAID IT LAST NIGHT.` · `MORNING'S WORDS, TURNED TO DUSK.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · `WORDS OF SHELTER.` · then, large: `EVENING, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Listen for one evening sound near you: a car passing, a fan, a voice in another room, your own breath. Stay with that single sound for the sit, and when your attention drifts, come back to it. If you pray, you can say the line of refuge from Sahih Muslim once before you begin.
screen: `ONE EVENING SOUND.` · `STAY WITH IT.` · `COME BACK WHEN YOU DRIFT.`

howItsDone: Muslims who keep the evening adhkar recite set remembrances from the hadith between 'Asr and Maghrib or after Maghrib, including the last three short surahs of the Qur'an three times and the line of refuge from the hadith of the scorpion.

options: They're a request to God for shelter each evening, not a lucky charm.
Yes, it's a guaranteed shield. Say them and you never need to lock up.

chat.meaning: The evening adhkar ask God for refuge as the day ends. Shelter is asked for, from God; it isn't a spell.

adhkar.meaning: remembrances: short set phrases recalling God

Dadi.meaning: grandmother (father's mother), in Urdu and Hindi

Sahih Muslim.meaning: a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

Abu Dawud.meaning: a classical hadith scholar; his Sunan is a major collection

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2709 (the scorpion sting; 'I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He created')
Sahih Muslim 2723 (we have entered the evening, and the dominion belongs to God)
Sunan Abu Dawud 5082 (al-Ikhlas and the two chapters of refuge, three times evening and morning, suffice)
